title: I might be in the minority, I didn't particularly like "My Left Foot", though it did have its positives. It just felt too Oscar baity.

commenti.body:
Although Brenda Fricker was outstanding, she didn't have to have much range to play her role, while Day-Lewis, well, there's no point in echoing all the accolades he's received for that portrayal.

Have you ever spent any time around someone with cerebral palsy? Have you spent any time around disabled people at all? Have you spent any time around addicts? Have you spent any time around anyone who has been disabled, an addict, and a victim of abuse? I ask because it sounds like you're totally inexperienced in these areas, and have zero idea of what it looks like in real life.

Your perspective seems extremely limited, and this post seems too showy and even forced, like you're aiming to demean someone playing a disabled person, using the most middle of the road criticism of "it felt too Oscar baity." Trying to mask that intent by pretending to lift the female performers. . . to where they were already recognized - Brenda Fricker won the Oscar for her portrayal - doesn't quite cover the ignorance you seem to lead with here. Unnecessary, terrible take.

I find myself feeling this way about this whole era of biopic films. There is a certain delivery that once I had seen a million of them, I really have trouble fully embracing them now. So I get what you are saying with the "Oscar bait" comment.

I haven't rewatched My Left Foot since I was younger and like a lot of these types of movies I am in no rush to do so and would rather hold on to my initial reaction and feelings about it. 

I think there are certainly exceptions, and some are way better than others. Sometimes, I'm more able to embrace the shmaltzy sort of overdone feelings they present to me and watch this kimd of film but usually I find myself distanced from the heartwrenching charachter drama they desperately want me to feel.

I don't know if I just grew jaded or if these sorts of films really are just as interchangable as I feel.

It was probably the film to usher in modern "Oscar Bait" disability performances following Rainmain, and Daniel Day Lewis beat out Tom Cruise in a wheelchair that year. It was also the year that Hollywood decided that they ended racism by giving Denzel an Oscar and celebrating an old bigot's transformation into slightly less of a bigot with Driving Miss Daisy winning Best Picture.

If you look ahead to the ableist Oscar bait of the following few years -  Regarding Henry, Awakenings, Benny & Joon, What's Eating Gilbert Grape, just to name a few - My Left Foot seems almost restrained. 

But yeah, it's dated.
Omg I haven't even thought of a couple of these in ages. Ironically Regarding Henry had completely slipped my mind, but now I can picture Harrison Ford in it way too clearly.

I feel like this is the first modern Oscar bait movie. There’s been a lot of imitators since. I don’t think it’s bad and Daniel Day Lewis is phenomenal in almost anything he’s in but I’m not crazy about it either. In the Name of the Father is far better and his performance is a little more dynamic.

That and *Awakenings* were both directed with a specific "drool a bit and then get angry like Frankenstein's monster when he sees fire" intensity. *Awakenings* was the better of the two and touching in a smalzy "Only-Penny-Marshall-Can-Make-This-Work" kind of way. Or maybe Robin Williams sold it. But *Regarding Henry* (written by JJ Abrams) had all the subtelty of hitting someone over the head with an Oscar statue. No idea how Harrison Ford thought "Asshole lawyer suffers a brain injury and becomes a nice guy" was going to win anyone over.
He was brilliant in My Beautiful Laundrette.

Sorry but boo to this post. OP was not necessarily saying it was wasn’t an accurate portrayal of someone with cerebral palsy. They were saying that such a portrayal does not fully showcase a range of nuanced emotions, which is maybe more difficult to pull off well. For me personally, nuanced performances are certainly more interesting. I have no idea to what exact degree this Lewis performance is an accurate portrayal of someone with cerebral palsy. I’m sure it’s rather close. But i personally don’t find this kind of performance as nearly as compelling as say, Joaquin Phoenix in the Master (to choose something at random)

Let the OP speak for themselves.

Like the OP, it also sounds like you don't find the limits of some disabled people interesting enough to view a story about them.

Having a preference is different than suggesting a portrayal is "very hammy" or "too showy and even forced" or "Oscar baity". It's similar to a transphobic person saying a gay character is "too flamboyant" or a racist saying a black character is "too ghetto". It's plain ignorance.
Thank god the movie Radio was so bad it ruined that “genre.”

You might not but perhaps there are people, such as Christy, who live their every day life with extreme emotion.

I thought it was a very good movie, but like any movie, it isn’t for everyone.

Been a while since I saw it but I remember it feeling a bit BBC drama as you say. 

Not so much Lewis’s performance particularly, but the whole way it was scripted and shot. Very by the numbers. I feel like it could have done with a more documentary feel. A bit looser, a bit less formally constructed, both in the writing and camera work/editing.
"Get angry like Frankenstein when he sees fire" 🤣

Personally, I find that there’s no phrase as meaningless in the discourse around movies than “Oscar bait.”

It’s a phrase that engenders a brand of cynicism that requires absolutely no proof, while ironically being quite self-assured in its proclamation. Actually, it’s a *position* more than a commentary or critique, and it rarely leads to interesting conversations about film because it’s steeped in assumptions about motivations that can’t be known unless the creators involved explicitly say so in an interview. 

Fact is, just about everyone working in the industry would love to put an Oscar on the mantle, and they do the best work they can in service of the project and its potential (in the box office *and* the awards circuit). So in effect, it’s all Oscar bait. And when it’s all Oscar bait, none of it is. 

*My Left Foot* strikes me as earnest without being sentimental, emotional without being maudlin, and sincere without being self-conscious as piece of art. It’s a great film.

I don't know why you're analysing a genre based on the genre name, that's not how genres work.

"Oscar bait" is something between an observation and accusation, categorising films which are sentimental, saccharine, mediocre drama films about social topics like racism, disability, injustice, alcoholism etc. Which intentionally seek to challenge the audience as little as possible.

Prove “intentionally.” I think people who make movies do the best they can, and sometimes their reach exceeds their grasp. Often they’re not as talented as they want to be or think they are, and sometimes they chase trends and that screws them over. 

But these accusations of “intentionally” making something worse than it needs to be are not only baseless and reflexively cynical (the *cheap* kind of cynical, because you don’t have to show your homework), they expose the accusers as having no idea how the process works.

As an editor for twenty years, I’ve published a wide range of talent, and everyone single one of them, from the obscure to the New York Times Bestsellers, were doing the very best they could. Some were more talented than others, but they never, ever put in less than their best effort. 

One thing I’ve learned is that it’s easier to shit on that effort than take the time to understand what goes into it.
